title: Role-Play & Simulation

pts: Role-play assigns learners a specific character and situation to act out, often briefly.
Simulation runs a more extended, realistic scenario where learners act largely as themselves within structured constraints.
Both generate communicative pressure that abstract exercises rarely can.

items: Give teachers two cards describing the same situation: one written as a role-play, one as a simulation (see model language).
In pairs, teachers list the differences: who the learner ‘is’, how long it lasts, what the outcome is, how much acting is needed.
Discuss which version suits which class, and why.
Each pair rewrites a textbook dialogue as either a role-play or a short simulation.
Try both versions with a class in successive weeks and compare the talk they produce.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Role-play: You are Mr Reddy. You bought a pressure cooker last week and the handle is loose. Go back to the shop and get it replaced. Your partner is the shopkeeper.
Simulation: Your class has ₹5,000 from the school fund for one improvement. In groups of five, study three quotations, agree on one choice and present it to the headteacher (played by the teacher).

blocks.x: In the first, the learner acts a character for five minutes. In the second, learners act largely as themselves across a whole lesson, with a real decision to reach.

body: Purpose: to show the distinction. Content: two panels. On the left, a learner holding a theatrical mask, labelled ‘Role-play: a character, a scene’. On the right, the same learner wearing a name badge at a meeting table with papers, labelled ‘Simulation: yourself, a situation’. Style: clean, friendly. Board version: a mask and a badge drawn side by side.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared bank of scenario cards.

blocks.x: Scenario cards handwritten on index cards.

pts: A role card gives a character's goals and key information without scripting exact language to use.
Too much scripted detail collapses the task into recitation, losing the genuine communicative negotiation.
Too little detail leaves learners without enough to work with — calibrate against the class's proficiency level.

items: Decide the situation and the two characters.
For each character, write three things: who you are, what you want, what you know that the other person does not.
Remove any complete sentences for learners to say; keep only information and goals.
Check the level: add one or two key words at lower levels; add a hidden complication at higher levels.
Pilot the cards with two learners before using them with the class.
Learners write role cards for each other once they understand the format.
Support: add a short ‘useful words’ box to the card.
Challenge: add a secret constraint (You must leave in ten minutes).

blocks.x: Card A (written for this book): You are a passenger at Mysuru bus stand. You want to reach Madikeri before 6 p.m. You have ₹300. You do not like night buses. Card B: You work at the enquiry counter. The next direct bus leaves at 4.30 p.m. and costs ₹260. A faster private bus leaves at 5.15 p.m. and costs ₹350. Too much detail: Say ‘Excuse me, what time is the next bus to Madikeri?’ This turns the task into reading aloud. Too little detail: You want a bus. This leaves weaker learners with nothing to say.

body: Purpose: to show what a good role card contains. Content: a single card with three labelled sections, ‘Who you are’, ‘What you want’, ‘What only you know’, and a small crossed-out speech bubble showing a scripted sentence. Style: clear, annotated. Board version: a rectangle divided into three.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for printable card templates.

blocks.x: Cards cut from old notebook covers or chart paper.

body: Write role cards in the second person (You are… You want…) and keep them to about forty words. Learners should be able to read a card, turn it over and remember what they want.

pts: The most productive role-plays involve some conflict or gap between characters' goals that must be resolved through talk.
This connects directly to Unit 30's negotiation-of-meaning principles, generated through imagined rather than real content.
A role-play with no real tension quickly becomes a stilted, low-value exercise.

v: Paired role cards with conflicting goals

items: Pair learners and give each a card with a goal that conflicts with the partner’s.
Set a clear outcome: the pair must reach an agreement, or agree that they cannot.
Allow the interaction to run for five to seven minutes.
Pairs report their outcome in one sentence to the class.
Compare outcomes: how did different pairs solve the same conflict?
Use three-person scenarios with a mediator whose goal is to find a compromise.
Support: reduce the conflict to one point of difference.
Challenge: add a second point of difference so learners must trade concessions.

blocks.x: Conflict (written for this book): A (parent): You want your daughter home by 7 p.m. B (daughter, 16): Your friend’s birthday party ends at 9 p.m. Possible exchange:

lines: A: Seven o’clock. That’s final.
B: But Amma, everyone’s staying till nine. What if Priya’s father drops me home?
A: Hmm. What time exactly?
B: By nine fifteen. I promise I’ll call you at eight.

blocks.x: Learners must ask, clarify and propose, which are the moves of negotiation of meaning (Unit 30). A role-play in which both characters agree from the start produces a polite, short and low-value exchange.

body: Purpose: to show conflict as the engine of interaction. Content: two characters on either side of a gap, each holding a sign with their goal; a bridge made of speech bubbles is being built between them. Style: warm, slightly humorous. Board version: two stick figures and a bridge.

items: Wordwall (free basic version) to randomly assign scenario pairs.

blocks.x: Paired cards in envelopes, one envelope per bench.

pts: Give learners brief individual preparation time to understand their role before the interaction begins.
Keep the in-character phase focused on communication, saving language correction for after, per Unit 8's delayed-correction principle.
A short debrief afterward, out of character, surfaces language points naturally.

items: Preparation (5 minutes): each learner reads the card alone and notes key words; learners with the same role may prepare together in any language.
In character (8–10 minutes): pairs interact. The teacher circulates and notes useful language and common errors, without interrupting.
Step out: say clearly ‘Now you are yourselves again.’
Debrief (10 minutes): pairs discuss how it went; the teacher writes five or six anonymous sentences on the board, some good and some to improve.
Pairs repeat the role-play with new partners, using what they learned.
Swap roles for the repeat, so each learner experiences both sides.
Support: allow longer preparation and a short key-word list on the card.
Challenge: shorten preparation time to push spontaneous speech.

lines: ‘I want that you change it’ → I’d like you to change it.
Good: ‘Could you check again, please?’
Missing: a way to end politely (‘Thanks for your help’).

blocks.x: Debrief questions: Did you get what you wanted? What was hard to say? What did your partner say that was useful? Delayed correction (Unit 8) protects the flow of the interaction; the repeat lets learners use the correction straight away.

body: Purpose: to show the lesson shape. Content: three doors in a row. The first, ‘Prepare’, shows a learner reading a card; the second, ‘In character’, shows two learners talking with small theatre masks; the third, ‘Step out’, shows the same learners without masks, looking at the board. Style: simple, sequential. Board version: three boxes with arrows.

items: Classroomscreen (free basic version) for visible timers for each phase.

blocks.x: Phase times written on the board, with a clap to change phase.

pts: Apply Unit 33's genre awareness to the role-play's spoken genre — a job interview has different structural expectations than a casual complaint.
Briefly reviewing the genre's typical stages before the role-play raises the authenticity of what learners produce.
This turns role-play into a genre-practice tool, not just a fluency-only activity.

v: A short model of the spoken genre (live or recorded)

items: Choose a spoken genre for the role-play, such as a job interview or a complaint.
Play or perform a short model (written for this book, or a recording made with a colleague).
Learners identify the stages and the typical language in each stage.
Build a stage chart on the board.
Learners do the role-play, then check which stages they included.
Compare the same genre in English and in a home language: does a Kannada or Hindi job interview follow the same stages?
Support: give the stage chart with example phrases.
Challenge: learners identify the stages without the chart.

blocks.x: Stages of a service complaint (from Unit 33’s approach to spoken genres):

lines: 1. Greeting and opening (Good morning. I bought this here last week.)
2. Stating the problem (The screen has stopped working.)
3. Evidence (Here’s the bill.)
4. Request (Could I have a replacement, please?)
5. Negotiation (If you can’t replace it, could you repair it?)
6. Closing (Thank you. I’ll come back on Friday.)

blocks.x: A job interview has different stages and a more formal register. Knowing the genre lets learners sound realistic rather than simply fluent.

body: Purpose: to show the stages of a spoken genre. Content: a path with six stepping stones across a river, each labelled with a stage of a complaint and a short example phrase; a shop on the far bank. Style: map-like, clear. Board version: six numbered boxes in a line.

items: Vocaroo (free) or a phone voice recorder for recording a model dialogue.

blocks.x: The teacher and a learner perform the model live.

pts: A simulation can run across a full lesson or several lessons — a business negotiation, a mock conference, a community planning meeting.
This connects naturally to Unit 36's project-based learning, especially for simulations with a documented final outcome.
Extended simulations sustain motivation well because the stakes feel cumulative rather than a single isolated task.

v: Background sheets; role badges; a map of the locality

items: Lesson 1: introduce the problem (for example, where to put a new bus shelter). Learners read background sheets and form interest groups (shopkeepers, parents, elderly residents, the municipal engineer).
Groups prepare their position, arguments and questions.
Lesson 2: the meeting. A learner chair runs the agenda; groups present and question each other.
Groups negotiate and vote on a proposal.
Lesson 3: groups write the meeting minutes and a letter to the municipal office, which become the documented outcome.
Other scenarios: a school sports day planning meeting, a mock press conference, a village water committee.
Support: interest groups with more members share the speaking.
Challenge: introduce a mid-simulation ‘news update’ that changes the facts.

blocks.x: Background (written for this book): The municipality will build one bus shelter on Gandhi Road. Option A is outside the school gate. Option B is near the vegetable market. Option C is near the hospital. Chair’s language:

lines: Let’s begin. Item one is the location. Who would like to speak first?
Thank you. Does anyone have a question for the shopkeepers?

blocks.x: Because the simulation produces a written outcome, it overlaps with project-based learning (Unit 36). Stakes feel cumulative: what is said in Lesson 2 shapes what is written in Lesson 3.

body: Purpose: to show an extended scenario. Content: a timeline with three panels: groups reading background sheets at benches; a meeting with a chair, badges and a map; a finished letter and set of minutes pinned to a noticeboard. Style: narrative, colourful. Board version: three boxes labelled ‘Prepare’, ‘Meet’, ‘Record’.

items: Google Maps (free) for a real local map as background.
Padlet (free plan) for each group’s position statement.

blocks.x: A hand-drawn map of the locality on chart paper.

pts: Some learners are uncomfortable with performative role-play; simulation, closer to their real selves, often suits them better.
Offer an observer or note-taker role as a lower-pressure way to participate for particularly reluctant learners.
This connects to Unit 22's willingness-to-communicate model — reluctance is contextual, not a fixed trait to work around permanently.

items: Offer a range of roles: main speakers, advisers who whisper suggestions, observers with a checklist, a note-taker or reporter.
Let reluctant learners choose a lower-exposure role for the first round.
Give observers a real job: note three useful phrases and one moment where communication broke down.
In the next round, invite observers to move one step towards speaking (for example, as an adviser).
Over several weeks, notice whether learners move towards more active roles.
Use simulations where learners act as themselves; many reluctant actors are comfortable here.
Support: observers may take notes in their home language.
Challenge: the reporter summarizes the role-play for the class in one minute.

lines: Phrase I heard that was useful: … Moment when someone did not understand: … How they solved it: … Did the characters reach an agreement? Yes / No

blocks.x: A learner who refuses to ‘act’ is not necessarily unwilling to communicate. Willingness to communicate depends on the situation (MacIntyre et al. 1998; Unit 22), so changing the situation often changes the learner.

body: Purpose: to show graded participation. Content: a stage with two speakers in the centre; around it, rings of learners: advisers close to the stage, observers with clipboards further out, and a reporter at the edge with a notebook. Small arrows show learners moving inwards over time. Style: gentle, inclusive. Board version: concentric circles.

items: Google Forms (free) for observer checklists where devices are available.

pts: Assess communicative achievement of the character's goal, alongside language accuracy and appropriacy.
Sociolinguistic competence (Unit 27) is especially visible and assessable in role-play's register-sensitive scenarios.
Keep assessment criteria visible to learners beforehand so the performative element doesn't distort what's actually being judged.

items: Share a three-part rubric before the role-play: goal achievement, language accuracy, appropriacy.
Explain each part with an example.
Learners do the role-play; the teacher or peers use the rubric.
Give each learner a score or comment on each part separately.
Learners choose one part to improve in the next role-play.
Peer observers use one criterion each, then combine their feedback.
Support: use a simple yes / partly / not yet scale.
Challenge: add a criterion for managing the conversation (openings, closings, repair).

blocks.x: A three-part rubric (written for this book):

lines: Goal: Did you get what your character wanted, or a fair compromise?
Accuracy: Were your sentences clear and mostly correct?
Appropriacy: Did you speak politely enough for the situation and the person?

blocks.x: Appropriacy is where sociolinguistic competence (Unit 27) becomes visible. Give me my money back may be accurate, but it is too blunt for most shop counters. Acting skill is not on the rubric: a shy learner who achieves the goal politely should score well. Unit 46 develops performance assessment further.

body: Purpose: to show separate criteria. Content: three stage spotlights shining on a pair of speakers, each light labelled ‘Goal’, ‘Accuracy’ and ‘Appropriacy’. A fourth, switched-off light is labelled ‘Acting’. Style: theatrical, clear. Board version: three columns on the board.

items: Google Classroom (free) rubrics attached to a speaking task.

blocks.x: A rubric slip for each pair.

body: Take one dialogue from your textbook. Turn it into two role cards with opposite goals and no scripted sentences. Run it using the three phases in point 4, and compare the talk with what you hear when learners perform the original dialogue.

dek: Unit 38 of 100: structured imagined scenarios generate authentic-feeling communication with lower real-world stakes — a powerful, underused integration technique.

aims.x: This unit looks at role-play and simulation: structured, imagined situations in which learners use English to get something done. Both techniques bring into the classroom kinds of talk that are otherwise hard to practise, such as complaining, negotiating, persuading or being interviewed, while keeping the real-world stakes low.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: distinguish role-play from simulation and choose between them for a purpose;
write role cards that give goals and information without scripting language;
build a genuine conflict or information gap into a scenario;
run a role-play in clear phases: preparation, in-character interaction and debrief;
use genre knowledge to raise the realism of spoken role-play;
plan an extended simulation across several lessons;
support learners who are reluctant to act;
assess role-play for goal achievement, accuracy and appropriacy.

why: Why this matters. Some real-world communication — negotiating, complaining, interviewing — is hard to practise authentically in a classroom. Role-play makes it accessible safely.

background.x: Role-play has been part of communicative teaching since its beginnings. William Littlewood (1981) placed it among the ‘social interaction activities’ that move learners from controlled practice towards free communication, and Gillian Porter Ladousse (1987) showed how a wide range of role-plays could be built from simple starting points. Ken Jones (1982) drew a sharper line: in a simulation, participants are not acting a part for an audience but taking on functions and responsibilities within a structured reality, usually as themselves. A learner playing an angry customer is in a role-play; a learner who, as herself, joins a committee deciding where to build a new school toilet block is in a simulation. The distinction matters because it changes how much performing is involved, and therefore how comfortable different learners feel.

Why do these techniques work? Much of what learners need to say in English lies outside the classroom’s natural range of talk. The classroom offers questions and answers, explanations and instructions; it rarely offers the chance to refuse a request politely, argue about a bill or answer questions at a job interview. Role-play and simulation create the conditions for these kinds of talk: a purpose, a relationship between speakers, and a problem to solve. When characters want different things, learners must negotiate meaning (Unit 30), choose an appropriate register (Unit 27) and manage a spoken genre from beginning to end (Unit 33). Crookall and Oxford (1990) collected evidence and practice showing that well-designed simulations can sustain rich, extended language use.

In Indian classrooms, role-play is often already familiar in one form: learners memorize and perform a dialogue from the textbook. This unit argues for something different. A memorized dialogue is useful for pronunciation and confidence, but it is recitation, not communication. The NCF 2023 encourages drama, role-play and experiential learning as ways of making language use meaningful (NCERT 2023), and the NEP 2020 calls for pedagogy that is experiential and discussion-based (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). Scenarios drawn from learners’ lives, such as a ration shop, a bus depot enquiry, a panchayat meeting or a call to a mobile network helpline, make English feel usable. Home languages have a place too: learners can plan in Kannada or Tamil and perform in English, or play a bilingual interpreter whose job is to mediate between two characters.

items: Goal achievement. Record whether each pair reaches its character’s goal or a reasonable compromise.
Appropriacy check. Note three moments per lesson where register was well or poorly judged, and use them in the debrief.
Genre stages. Learners tick the stages of the spoken genre they included, and the teacher checks a sample.
Simulation outcome. Assess the documented product (minutes, letter, proposal) alongside the spoken meeting.
When you have used role-play, was it communication or recitation?
Which real-world spoken situations do your learners most need to practise?
How do you build conflict or information gaps into scenarios?
Which learners resist acting? What role might suit them better?
Do you correct during role-plays? What happens to the talk when you do?
What would a three-lesson simulation look like in your context?

terms.def: The suitability of a word, phrase or style for its context, purpose and audience; a sentence can be grammatically correct but inappropriate, such as an overly direct request to a principal.
The final stage of a role-play or simulation, in which learners discuss how it went and the teacher gives feedback on language and task performance.
Correcting errors after an activity has finished rather than during it, so that learners can focus on fluency and communication.
An activity in which learners hold different information and must communicate to complete a task, such as finding differences between two pictures or completing a timetable.

A card giving a learner the information needed to take part in a role-play, such as who they are, what they want and any constraints. Different cards for each partner create an information or opinion gap.

A speaking activity in which learners take on roles, often with role cards, and act out a situation such as a shop conversation or a meeting with a doctor. It lets learners rehearse language for situations beyond the classroom.

An extended activity in which learners act within a realistic, structured situation, such as a village panchayat meeting or a news studio, often keeping their own views and drawing on information provided.

A recognizable type of spoken interaction with a social purpose and typical stages, such as storytelling, service encounters or gossip (Eggins and Slade 1997). Mapping its stages gives learners a structure for unpredictable talk.

A learner’s readiness to enter into communication in a second language at a particular time with particular people (MacIntyre et al. 1998). It is influenced by confidence, anxiety and the classroom climate.
